title: The big lookout
hook: from a carpenter's town to Rome, from a seed to a creed: look back at the hill you've climbed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Romans, Phoebe the deacon and a list of names nobody reads, and your line was every name is someone. Did you thank someone by name? Day three hundred thirty-one.

Anyone who has hiked a long trail knows the moment. You've been looking at your boots for hours: the next rock, the next root, the next switchback. Then the path opens out onto a ledge, and you turn around. And there it all is. The parking lot, tiny. The river you crossed. The steep bit that nearly made you quit. You can't believe you walked all that. That's today. Three hundred thirty-one days ago you started at the bottom of this hill with one small word. Today we stop at the big lookout, turn around, and look back at the whole climb, before the path goes on.
screen: `LOOKING AT YOUR BOOTS FOR HOURS.` → `THE PATH OPENS ONTO A LEDGE.` → `YOU TURN AROUND.`

segments.voice: Camp one was first words. Amen, a word you'd said a thousand times. Grace, a gift you didn't earn. The Lord's Prayer, one line a day: our Father, thy kingdom come, daily bread, forgive us, deliver us. Agape. The cross. Easter morning, and the women at the tomb first. Camp two was the stories. A sower flinging seed on every kind of ground. A father running down the road. A girl in Nazareth, a carpenter's town nobody expected anything from. A road through Galilee, a last week in Jerusalem, and then Acts, the story carrying on, all the way to a shipwreck and to Rome. Camp three was the practices: ways to pray, Advent candles and the circle of the year, Sabbath, singing, giving, the sacraments, and a rule of life. Camp four was one Gospel, Mark, read in order, breathless, from the first line to the empty tomb and the young man's words: he's going ahead of you to Galilee. And camp five went deep: the Sermon on the Mount, the mystics, the whole family of churches, the creeds that grew from that seed, and these last three weeks, Paul's letter to Rome. From a mustard seed to a creed said by churches around the world. Paul, writing from prison, far along his own long road, wrote to his friends in Philippi, in the King James Bible: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." The mark. The target. Remember hamartia, sin as missing the mark? Paul's answer isn't to stop aiming. It's to keep pressing on. That's where year two begins: the whole Bible, in order, from its first line.
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMP FOUR: MARK, IN ORDER.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS, AND ROMANS.` · then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the one line you'll carry into year two. Settle, and breathe. Let the whole year pass in front of you, like the view from the lookout. Which line stayed with you? Maybe one of the carries: fear buries things, but now, nothing can separate us. Maybe a verse. Maybe something you realized on your own, on an ordinary Tuesday. Don't choose the most impressive one. Choose the one that's actually yours. After the bell, write it down somewhere you'll see it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the climb so far. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The ledge at the end of year one, where you turn around, see the whole climb, and then face the path ahead.
Your line: the hill goes on. Today, put your one line where you'll see it tomorrow morning: on the fridge, the mirror, your phone. Year two starts at the very beginning. Day three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Many Christians mark the end of a season or a year with a time of looking back, sometimes called an examen or a year's review, giving thanks for what has passed before setting out again.

fork.setup: you're Paul, writing from prison to friends in Philippi. you look back on everything. what do you say?
options: I've arrived; there's nothing left to climb.
forgetting what's behind, I press toward the mark.
I wish I'd taken an easier road.
fork.reveal: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." the hill goes on.

original.note: Greek: the mark, the goal you keep your eyes on. the root of our word scope.

trapdoor: what you thought: the big lookout is the end of the climb.
what it means: a place to stop, turn around, see the whole year, and then face the path ahead.
what a scholar hears: in Philippians 3:14 Paul says he pursues the skopos, the mark, the same picture of aiming that hides in hamartia, missing the mark.

sources.quoted: forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark

notes: Year close and camp five close. The camp summary names items from the year-one outline (camp 1 index; camps 2–5 in y1.md); confirm they match what the listener actually heard, especially if the outline changes.

Philippians is traditionally placed near the end of Paul's life (Roman imprisonment), though some scholars date it earlier (Ephesus). Softened: script now says 'writing from prison, far along his own long road' (imprisonment is stated in Philippians 1:13; the place and date are debated).
The link between skopos (Philippians 3:14) and hamartia (day 313) is the script's own connection, not an etymological one; the trapdoor says 'the same picture of aiming'. Confirm.
'A creed said by churches around the world': the Nicene Creed is used by Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant churches, though some Protestant traditions don't use creeds. Confirm wording.
